bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Global trade policy and tariff exposure / geopolitical developments — Named first in the MD&A Risk Management section as 'exposure to global trade policy changes and geopolitical developments'. It is not theoretical for FY 2025-26: the MD&A states 'Elevated U.S. tariff conditions and temporary disruptions across export markets created pressure on customer procurement patterns and revenue realisation', and the Chairman describes ordering patterns that 'remained subdued' for much of the year. Structural because exports are a large share of the business and the largest export market is the one where tariffs bit. Mitigation cited: strengthening geographic and business diversification and expanding customer relationships across new sectors.
- Customer concentration within core aerospace programmes — Explicitly listed as a key risk in the MD&A Risk Management section. The customer base is small and programme-linked — the Chairman states the Company serves 'approximately 35 customers across North America, Europe and India', and the BRSR (sibling bundle) records that a single activity, manufacturing relating to aero engine tooling and airframe tooling, accounts for 98% of turnover with clientele predominantly global OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers. Long qualification cycles cut both ways: they raise switching costs but also make any programme loss slow to replace. PROVENANCE: the 98% single-activity and OEM/Tier-1 clientele figures are back-filled from the BRSR Section A tables, which are present in the profile and governance_entities bundles, not in this one.
- Stringent regulatory and certification requirements — Listed as a key risk in the MD&A. Aerospace, defence and nuclear work is gated by certification and qualification regimes; the BRSR stakeholder table records engagement with governmental bodies and authorities to ensure 'compliance with aerospace and defense regulations, environmental requirements, and safety certification standards'. Mitigation cited: maintaining globally recognised quality systems.
- Integration risk from strategic initiatives / inorganic expansion — Named in the MD&A as 'integration risks associated with strategic initiatives'. The Company is simultaneously integrating and scaling Hobel Bellows (a listed MD&A priority, adding approximately 290 employees), standing up the Saudi JV, and has incorporated Uniflux Renewable Energy — three unrelated integration efforts running at once, in businesses (bellows/metal forming, remanufacturing, renewable-energy EPC) adjacent to but distinct from the tooling core.
- Operational complexity of a high-mix, low-volume manufacturing environment — Named in the MD&A as 'operational complexities arising from a high-mix manufacturing environment'. The Company describes a qualified ecosystem of more than 5,900 SKUs and 'complex, high-mix, low-volume production', which raises scheduling, tooling-changeover and quality-traceability burden per unit of revenue. Mitigation cited: ERP, MES deployment, CMM-integrated quality systems and monitoring of machining efficiency through a right-first-time approach and dispatch-cycle discipline.
- Cybersecurity and digital-adoption risk — Named in the MD&A as 'increasing cybersecurity considerations linked to digital adoption', and echoed in the Board's Report risk policy which explicitly lists cyber risk. It matters because the Company's model depends on secure digital systems for customer collaboration, documentation exchange and quality traceability, and clients themselves raised 'the importance of data security' in the BRSR stakeholder engagement table. Mitigation cited: continued investment in digital infrastructure, predictive maintenance, advanced analytics and cybersecurity infrastructure.
- Very high employee attrition and dependence on specialised technical talent — A structural concentration risk the AR discloses without labelling it a risk: the BRSR turnover-rate table records permanent-employee turnover of 49.06% in FY 2025-26 (57.53% in FY 2024-25) and permanent-worker turnover of 13.79% (75.00% in FY 2024-25). The MD&A itself calls the workforce 'a key competitive advantage' resting on 'specialised technical expertise', and the industry outlook names 'availability of skilled talent' as a key industry challenge. The Company also churned its Company Secretary twice inside two years. Mitigation cited: structured onboarding, cross-functional training, performance-linked incentives, ESOP-based employee ownership and an integrated HRMS. PROVENANCE: the turnover-rate percentages are back-filled from BRSR Section A item 22, present in the profile and governance_entities bundles, not in this one.
- Low capacity utilisation / operating-leverage risk after a capex-heavy year — The MD&A lists 'Improving capacity utilisation and operating leverage' as a forward priority and notes 'significant manufacturing headroom', while the Corporate Overview discloses capacity utilisation of 52% against installed capacity of 6.8 Lakh machine hours. Capacity was added into a soft-demand year — a precision components & assemblies facility and a fabrication facility commissioned in October, with a further 60,000 sq. ft. added in January 2026 — so fixed-cost absorption depends on the demand normalisation management describes as under way rather than as achieved. PROVENANCE: the 52% utilisation and facility dates are back-filled from the Corporate Overview 'Our Manufacturing Prowess' spread supplied in the capex_expansion bundle.
- Supplier / procurement concentration — The BRSR 'Openness of business' table records purchases from trading houses at 70% of total purchases (67% prior year) sourced from 78 trading houses versus 185 a year earlier, with the top 10 accounting for 41% of those purchases (34% prior year) — a materially narrower supplier base year on year. The MD&A industry commentary independently flags raw-material constraints, production bottlenecks and supply-chain vulnerability across the A&D ecosystem. PROVENANCE: the concentration percentages are back-filled from BRSR Principle 1 item 9, supplied in the capex_expansion bundle, not in this one.

outlook.body:
- Evolve beyond origins as an aerospace tooling company into an integrated precision engineering platform serving aerospace, defence, nuclear energy, semiconductors and industrial manufacturing.
- Expand capabilities beyond tooling into higher-value precision components, assemblies and fabricated products — the stated purpose of the dedicated precision components & assemblies facility and fabrication facility commissioned in October.
- Capability-led acquisitions: the Hobel Bellows acquisition expands presence beyond precision-machined components into higher-value engineered assemblies and subsystems, adding metal forming, bellows manufacturing, fabrication and assembly solutions, with identified commercial and operational synergies enabling more integrated solutions, larger work packages and cross-selling across both businesses.
- Build a strong position in nuclear energy — leveraging India's ambition to reach ~100 GW installed nuclear capacity, new reactors and refurbishment programmes; management is 'committed to strengthening our capabilities in this area'.
- Strengthen position with leading global semiconductor equipment OEMs through sustained investments in advanced manufacturing capabilities and capability development.
- Expand international footprint and proximity to customers — the Kanoo-Unimech Joint Venture in Saudi Arabia (YBAK) to participate in opportunities emerging across the Middle East.
- FTWZ (Free Trade Warehousing Zone) strategy, alongside international expansion initiatives and capability-led acquisitions, to strengthen customer stickiness and improve long-term durability of the business.
- Deepen the associate/deep-tech position in advanced defence and propulsion technologies via an increased stake in Dheya Technologies, with commercial deployment of its propulsion platform subject to certifications, expanding customer adoption, developing next-generation higher-thrust engines and establishing dedicated testing infrastructure.
- Continue investing through the cycle in capabilities, customer relationships and future growth opportunities rather than reacting to short-term volatility; continued investment in talent, infrastructure and engineering excellence.
- Serve global OEMs and industry leaders through both build-to-print and build-to-specification models across design, manufacture and supply of high-precision products and systems.
- Diversify customer base and create multiple growth engines to underpin the Company's next phase of expansion.
- Diversify end markets across aerospace (flying and non-flying), semiconductors, energy (nuclear reactor modernisation and new-build, oil & gas) and defence.
- Stated philosophy is full reinvestment and a debt-free standalone balance sheet. DIVIDEND: 'With a view to conserve resources for the ongoing business operations and to finance strategic future growth initiatives, your Board has deemed it prudent not to recommend any dividend on the Equity Shares of the Company for the Financial Year ended March 31, 2026.' A Dividend Distribution Policy has been formulated under Regulation 43A of the Listing Regulations and is published on the Company's website. RESERVES: 'your Board has not proposed to transfer any amount to the General Reserve, and the entire balance of profit after tax has been retained in the Surplus / Retained Earnings account of the Company.' BORROWINGS: as of March 31, 2026 there are no long-term borrowings (non-current financial liabilities) and no short-term borrowings (current financial liabilities) on a standalone basis; the Company has not made any one-time settlement for loans taken from banks or financial institutions, and no deposits under Chapter V of the Act were accepted. SHARE CAPITAL: authorised capital Rs. 30,00,00,000 and issued/subscribed/paid-up equity capital Rs. 25,42,84,415 comprising 5,08,56,883 equity shares of face value Rs. 5 each, unchanged during the year — no differential-rights shares, sweat equity, bonus shares or ESOP allotments were issued, although 98,526 options were granted under the Unimech Employee Stock Option Plan, 2024. IPO PROCEEDS: the IPO of 63,69,426 equity shares of Rs. 5 each completed on December 31, 2024 for Rs. 500 Crores comprised a Fresh Issue of 31,84,713 shares at Rs. 785 per share (Rs. 250 Crores) and an Offer for Sale of the same size by the promoter/promoter group; shareholders approved a CHANGE IN THE OBJECTS OF THE ISSUE by postal ballot on December 17, 2025, and the Board's Report states gross fresh-issue proceeds of Rs. 250.00 Crores with Rs. 153.30 Crores utilised as per the objects of the issue and Rs. 96.70 Crores pending utilisation. FUTURE FUND-RAISING: Special Business item 3 of the Notice of the 10th AGM (Friday, August 28, 2026, 11:00 AM IST, via VC/OAVM) seeks a Special Resolution approving the raising of funds by way of a qualified institutions placement (QIP) to eligible investors through the issuance of securities; the resolution text is truncated in the routed extract before the size or terms are stated. DEPLOYMENT INTENT evidenced in the same reports: an approved investment of up to Rs. 450 Crores (with Innomech) for the Hobel Bellows acquisition, Rs. 552.51 Lakhs to raise the Dheya stake to 29.99%, a 51% JV commitment in Saudi Arabia, and incorporation of Uniflux Renewable Energy Private Limited. NOTE ON SCOPE: the section supplied under the heading '=== CORPORATE GOVERNANCE REPORT ===' does not contain the Corporate Governance Report — no board-meeting or attendance record, committee composition, directors' remuneration, shareholding pattern or means-of-communication disclosure is present anywhere in this bundle; that content is therefore not extractable here.
- Occupational health & safety: the Company operates an Occupational Health and Safety Management System aligned with ISO 45001:2018, subject to regular internal audits, statutory inspections, third-party assessments and ISO 45001:2018 surveillance audits. 100% of plants and offices were assessed for both health and safety practices and working conditions.
- Safety outcomes: 'During the reporting period, no major safety-related incidents or significant systemic risks were observed that required material corrective actions beyond routine improvements and preventive measures.' A formal CAPA process with root-cause analysis is in place, with findings reviewed by the HSE Committee and management for closure.
- Human rights: a comprehensive Human Rights Policy aligned with the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the principles of the UN Global Compact, covering employees, workers, contractors, suppliers and other stakeholders, with sub-policies on anti-discrimination, prohibition of child labour, forced and bonded labour, modern slavery and human trafficking, anti-harassment and abuse, freedom of association, migrant and foreign workers, women's rights, non-retaliation and whistleblowing.
- Human-rights training coverage: 100% of employees (81 permanent) and 100% of workers (22 permanent) were trained on human-rights issues in FY 2025-26, matching 100% coverage in FY 2024-25.
- Human-rights assessment coverage: 100% of plants and offices assessed for child labour, forced/involuntary labour, sexual harassment, discrimination at workplace and wages; 'no significant human rights risks or adverse findings were identified during the reporting period' and no major corrective action plans were required.
- Human rights in the supply chain: human-rights requirements form part of business agreements and contracts with suppliers, vendors, contractors and other business partners, including clauses prohibiting child labour, forced or bonded labour, discrimination, harassment and unfair employment practices.
- Wages: 100% of all permanent employees and workers — male and female — were paid more than the minimum wage in both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25; nil were paid at only the minimum wage.
- Gender pay footprint: gross wages paid to females were 5.41% of total wages in FY 2025-26, down from 13.23% in FY 2024-25. Median remuneration disclosure shows 9 female employees (other than BoD/KMP) at a median of INR 48,80,276 versus 68 male employees at INR 4,52,433, and 1 female worker at INR 77,580 versus 21 male workers at INR 1,05,466 — the Company reports these medians without explanation of the inversion at employee level.
- POSH: nil complaints reported, nil upheld and nil pending under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act in both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25; an Internal Complaints Committee is constituted, POSH compliance was strengthened through registration and reporting on the She-Box Portal, and a zero-retaliation approach is documented in a Non-Retaliation Policy.
- Grievance mechanisms: nil complaints filed in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25 across sexual harassment, discrimination at workplace, child labour, forced/involuntary labour, wages and other human-rights issues; dedicated committees cover canteen management, POSH, transportation, Health, Safety and Environment (HSE) and employee grievance redressal, supported by an Internal Monitoring System (IMS) spanning social, safety, security, HR and environmental compliance.
- CSR: the Company spent Rs. 22,89,809 (including a Government Contribution of Rs. 2,14,205) against a CSR obligation of Rs. 20,24,196 for the financial year ended March 31, 2026 — i.e. it spent above its obligation. Independent Directors met separately on February 27, 2026 to review the performance of the Board, its Chairman and Non-Independent Directors.
- Stakeholder engagement is formalised by group, channel and frequency: Employees (quarterly — feedback sought improved safety equipment and clearer career progression pathways), Suppliers (yearly / on OTD and quality basis — concerns on delivery timelines and raw-material specification clarity), Clients (quarterly — quality assurance, product customisation, timely delivery, with emphasis on data security), Governmental Bodies and Authorities (as required), and NGOs (annually, identified as the vulnerable & marginalised group channel, focused on local employment generation and infrastructure development). outlook.body:
- Structural expansion cycle in global aerospace & defence driven by commercial aviation growth, elevated defence spending and investment in fleet sustainment and modernisation.
- Passenger traffic projected to cross 10 Billion by CY 2026; passenger load factors have remained above 82%, reflecting high aircraft utilisation and pressure on airline fleets.
- Aircraft production constrained by material shortages, labour constraints and engine supply disruptions; large OEM order backlogs now extend into the next decade, delaying deliveries and compelling airlines to maximise utilisation of existing fleets — extending the MRO cycle.
- Global MRO market surpassed USD 136 Billion in CY 2025 and is projected to approach USD 193 Billion by the end of the decade; engine maintenance remains the largest MRO category.
- Narrow-body aircraft account for approximately 75-80% of global deliveries; production scale-up requires highly engineered assembly systems, precision tooling, structural jigs, component fixtures and automated manufacturing platforms.
- Company has established capabilities across next-generation engine platforms (LEAP 1A, LEAP 1B, Pratt & Whitney GTF, Rolls-Royce Trent XWB) expected to remain central to future aircraft deliveries; opportunity framed as the broader maintenance/aftermarket ecosystem rather than tooling as a standalone market.
- Durability concerns and premature wear in certain engine platforms have caused localised fleet groundings, generating incremental demand for teardown tooling, engine extraction systems and repair infrastructure.
- Passenger-to-Freighter (P2F) conversions expected to account for a significant share of fleet additions, requiring customised structural jigs, shoring systems, drilling templates, fastening tools and specialised assembly fixtures.
- Global GSE market estimated at over USD 10 billion in CY 2026 and expected to nearly double over the coming years, supported by airport expansion, fleet growth and infrastructure modernisation; transition towards electric GSE platforms and telematics-enabled operations.
- Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing aviation market and is expected to account for the largest share of future aircraft deliveries, driving localisation of manufacturing infrastructure, tooling ecosystems, MRO capacity and component supply chains.
- Global precision tooling market estimated at approximately USD 313.17 Billion in CY 2026, supported by multi-axis CNC deployment, predictive analytics and robotics-driven manufacturing.
- Global defence industry projected to grow from approximately USD 542.72 Billion in CY 2026 to over USD 739 Billion by CY 2035 (CAGR of more than 7%); active global military fleet expected to expand by approximately 13.4% over the coming decade.
- 'Friend-shoring' and 'China Plus One' supply-chain diversification creating long-term opportunities for precision tooling manufacturers in strategic markets such as India.
- Nuclear: international commitments target a threefold increase in global nuclear capacity by CY 2050; India targeting 100 GW of installed nuclear capacity by CY 2047, with new reactors, SMRs and NPCIL's En-Masse Coolant Channel Replacement (EMCCR) refurbishment programmes driving demand for high-precision engineering and specialised fabrication.
- Semiconductor manufacturing equipment market valued at approximately USD 166.35 Billion in CY 2025, projected to exceed USD 344 Billion by CY 2032 (CAGR approximately 11.0%); India's national semiconductor mission attracting investment across fabrication and ATMP infrastructure.
- Oil & gas: investments across LNG infrastructure, refining systems, drilling assets and industrial process systems supporting demand for precision-manufactured valves, pumps, turbine systems and pressure-control systems.
- Global energy demand transformation driven by industrialisation, AI data centres, semiconductor manufacturing growth and digital infrastructure, increasing demand for reliable baseload generation.
- Precision engineering: industry expected to adopt hybrid manufacturing (additive integrated with traditional machining), AI-enabled predictive maintenance and digital manufacturing ecosystems; the global precision engineering market is valued at over USD 100 billion.
- Company-specific headwind and its reversal: global trade uncertainties and tariff-related disruptions kept customer ordering patterns subdued for much of FY 2025-26, but business momentum improved meaningfully during the fourth quarter as customer confidence strengthened and ordering began to normalise; management views the softer demand as temporary.
- Management states the easing of tariff-related uncertainties in its largest export markets and gradual normalisation of customer ordering patterns are encouraging, with growing demand visibility across key sectors providing a favourable backdrop for future growth.
- Long qualification cycles, deep technical collaboration and consistent execution make Unimech an integral part of customers' supply chains, supporting resilience and long-term visibility.
- Stated industry challenges: high capital intensity and availability of skilled talent remain key challenges for the precision engineering industry.
- India macro backdrop: real GDP growth estimated between 7.4%-7.8% in FY 2025-26; PLI schemes, Atmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India supporting domestic industrial ecosystems; global GDP growth for CY 2026 projected at approximately 3.1%.
- Closed FY 2025-26 with a consolidated order book of over INR 200 Crores, stated to be the highest in the Company's history.
- Secured a USD 4 Million Ground Support Equipment (GSE) order under the LEAP engine programme — described as one of the largest orders in the Company's aero-tooling business history.
- Secured approximately INR 87 Crores of nuclear orders during the year while building a broader opportunity pipeline in that segment.
- Associate Dheya secured an initial order from a Defence Tier-1 customer for engine testing and validation, with potential for meaningful scale-up upon successful qualification.
- Customer engagement levels remain healthy across key segments, with encouraging momentum across aerospace, defence, nuclear energy, semiconductors and industrial applications.
- Serves approximately 35 customers across North America, Europe and India; strengthened participation within existing customer programmes and added new engagements across aerospace, energy, semiconductor and industrial applications.

risks.note: Named first in the MD&A Risk Management section as 'exposure to global trade policy changes and geopolitical developments'. It is not theoretical for FY 2025-26: the MD&A states 'Elevated U.S. tariff conditions and temporary disruptions across export markets created pressure on customer procurement patterns and revenue realisation', and the Chairman describes ordering patterns that 'remained subdued' for much of the year. Structural because exports are a large share of the business and the largest export market is the one where tariffs bit. Mitigation cited: strengthening geographic and business diversification and expanding customer relationships across new sectors.
risks.risk: Global trade policy and tariff exposure / geopolitical developments

risks.note: Explicitly listed as a key risk in the MD&A Risk Management section. The customer base is small and programme-linked — the Chairman states the Company serves 'approximately 35 customers across North America, Europe and India', and the BRSR (sibling bundle) records that a single activity, manufacturing relating to aero engine tooling and airframe tooling, accounts for 98% of turnover with clientele predominantly global OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers. Long qualification cycles cut both ways: they raise switching costs but also make any programme loss slow to replace. risks.note: Listed as a key risk in the MD&A. Aerospace, defence and nuclear work is gated by certification and qualification regimes; the BRSR stakeholder table records engagement with governmental bodies and authorities to ensure 'compliance with aerospace and defense regulations, environmental requirements, and safety certification standards'. Mitigation cited: maintaining globally recognised quality systems.

Named in the MD&A as 'integration risks associated with strategic initiatives'. The Company is simultaneously integrating and scaling Hobel Bellows (a listed MD&A priority, adding approximately 290 employees), standing up the Saudi JV, and has incorporated Uniflux Renewable Energy — three unrelated integration efforts running at once, in businesses (bellows/metal forming, remanufacturing, renewable-energy EPC) adjacent to but distinct from the tooling core.
risks.risk: Integration risk from strategic initiatives / inorganic expansion

risks.note: Named in the MD&A as 'operational complexities arising from a high-mix manufacturing environment'. The Company describes a qualified ecosystem of more than 5,900 SKUs and 'complex, high-mix, low-volume production', which raises scheduling, tooling-changeover and quality-traceability burden per unit of revenue. Mitigation cited: ERP, MES deployment, CMM-integrated quality systems and monitoring of machining efficiency through a right-first-time approach and dispatch-cycle discipline.
risks.risk: Operational complexity of a high-mix, low-volume manufacturing environment

risks.note: Named in the MD&A as 'increasing cybersecurity considerations linked to digital adoption', and echoed in the Board's Report risk policy which explicitly lists cyber risk. It matters because the Company's model depends on secure digital systems for customer collaboration, documentation exchange and quality traceability, and clients themselves raised 'the importance of data security' in the BRSR stakeholder engagement table. Mitigation cited: continued investment in digital infrastructure, predictive maintenance, advanced analytics and cybersecurity infrastructure.

A structural concentration risk the AR discloses without labelling it a risk: the BRSR turnover-rate table records permanent-employee turnover of 49.06% in FY 2025-26 (57.53% in FY 2024-25) and permanent-worker turnover of 13.79% (75.00% in FY 2024-25). The MD&A itself calls the workforce 'a key competitive advantage' resting on 'specialised technical expertise', and the industry outlook names 'availability of skilled talent' as a key industry challenge. The Company also churned its Company Secretary twice inside two years. Mitigation cited: structured onboarding, cross-functional training, performance-linked incentives, ESOP-based employee ownership and an integrated HRMS. PROVENANCE: the turnover-rate percentages are back-filled from BRSR Section A item 22, present in the profile and governance_entities bundles, not in this one.
risks.risk: Very high employee attrition and dependence on specialised technical talent
